literal: Fellow Ministers set out chicken-and-millet fare for him in a thatched hut; talkers held this high.
idiomatic: Ministerial colleagues served him plain chicken and millet in a thatched hut—men of taste admired it.

literal: At dawn, about to enter the ministry, he always saw his younger brother before leaving.
idiomatic: Before dawn, heading to the ministry, he always visited his brother first.

literal: A slave played pipa on horseback; Daoqian heard it and had the slave beaten a hundred strokes.
idiomatic: Hearing a slave play pipa on horseback, Daoqian had him beaten a hundred blows.

literal: The princess had two sons: Changyu and Changren.
idiomatic: The princess bore Changyu and Changren.

literal: Changyu was dull; Changren died young.
idiomatic: Changyu lacked wit; Changren died young.

literal: Daoqian also married a lady of the Sima clan and had Changyu.
idiomatic: He also married a Sima and had Changyu.

literal: Later the Sima lady was dismissed; he married again into the Yuan clan, very clever, and often lectured on the Laozi from a high seat.
idiomatic: Later he dismissed the Sima wife and married a clever Yuan who lectured on the Laozi from a high seat.

literal: His cousin Yuanming listened from behind a gauze curtain.
idiomatic: Cousin Yuanming listened behind a gauze screen.

literal: The Yuan lady bore two sons, Changsi and Changheng; Changheng was most renowned.
idiomatic: She bore Changsi and Changheng; Changheng was best known.

literal: Changheng, styled Zijun, childhood name Longzi.
idiomatic: Changheng, styled Zijun, childhood name Longzi.

literal: Calm and deep, with talent and insight; his spirit was elegant and light; bearing and deportment could serve as model.
idiomatic: Calm, perceptive, elegant in spirit—his bearing was a model.

literal: He ranged through classics and histories and was skilled in cursive and running script.
idiomatic: He read classics and histories and excelled at cursive and running script.

literal: His cousin Sidao, childhood name Shinu, was called the clan's wonder; Changheng was pushed with him.
idiomatic: Cousin Sidao, childhood name Shinu, was the clan's prodigy; Changheng stood beside him in renown.

literal: Hence a saying of You Province: "A thousand li of the Lu house—Shinu and Longzi."
idiomatic: You Province said: "A thousand li of Lu—Shinu and Longzi."

literal: " In Wei he served concurrently as Outside Army Aide to the Grand Minister of War.
idiomatic: Under Wei he was Outside Army Aide to the Grand Minister of War.

literal: When Qi received the mandate he served in succession as Magistrate of Ping'en.
idiomatic: When Qi took the throne he was Magistrate of Ping'en in turn.

literal: Right Vice Minister Zu Xiaozheng recommended him as Gentleman of the Ministry of Revenue.
idiomatic: Right Vice Minister Zu Xiaozheng made him Revenue Gentleman.

literal: Xiaozheng often said: "In appointing Lu Zijun Minister Gentleman I am clear before the living and the dead."
idiomatic: Xiaozheng said: "Using Lu Zijun as Minister Gentleman I owe nothing to living or dead."

literal: " From Tianbao on, Minister Wang Xin was punished for elegant talk; the younger brothers still held to it without falling away.
idiomatic: Since Tianbao, when Minister Wang Xin was punished for salon talk, the younger men still kept the tradition.

literal: From then this path gradually faded.
idiomatic: After that the fashion waned.

literal: Changheng with Li Ruo of Dunqiu, Liu Min of Pengcheng, Lu Yanshi of Henan, Xin Deyuan of Longxi, and Wang Xun were all rising men of elegant fashion.
idiomatic: Changheng, Li Ruo, Liu Min, Lu Yanshi, Xin Deyuan, and Wang Xun were the new salon set.

literal: Later he served concurrently as Regular Attendant and received Zhou envoys.
idiomatic: Later he was Regular Attendant greeting Zhou envoys.

literal: When Zhou Wu pacified Qi he was made Director of Jade, Middle Grade, and with Grand Minister of Ceremonies Husi Zheng revised the Rites Code.
idiomatic: When Zhou conquered Qi he was Director of Jade and with Husi Zheng revised the Rites Code.

literal: At the start of Sui Kaihuang he was made Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites.
idiomatic: Early in Sui Kaihuang he was Vice Minister of Rites.

literal: Emperor Wen once gathered his ministers and ordered each to state his merits; all competed to advance, but Changheng alone said nothing.
idiomatic: Wendi once gathered officials to boast of merit; all pushed forward but Changheng was silent.

literal: Left Vice Minister Gao Jiong looked at him with surprise.
idiomatic: Left Vice Minister Gao Jiong eyed him in wonder.

literal: Chen envoys He Che and Zhou Fen came in succession on embassy; the court always had Changheng receive them.
idiomatic: Chen envoys He Che and Zhou Fen came in turn; court always sent Changheng.

literal: Before long he went out as Chief Clerk to the Xuzhou Grand Governor; he had a great name for ability.
idiomatic: Soon he was chief clerk to Xuzhou's grand governor and famed for competence.

literal: Minister of Personnel Su Wei assessed him: "Virtue is the age's measure; conduct the gentleman's rule."
idiomatic: Su Wei of Personnel wrote: "His virtue is the age's yardstick; his conduct the gentleman's rule."

literal: " Discussants took it as a fine tale.
idiomatic: Talkers made a proverb of it.

literal: Once traveling to Junyi, the horse he rode was struck dead by another man's ox.
idiomatic: Passing Junyi, another man's ox killed his horse.

literal: The ox's owner apologized and asked to repay the value.
idiomatic: The owner apologized and offered payment.

literal: Changheng said: "When beasts collide it is ordinary rule—how is this a matter of human feeling? Why apologize?
idiomatic: Changheng said: "Beasts collide by nature—not a human affair. Why apologize?

literal: " He refused and would not accept.
idiomatic: He refused payment.

literal: His nature was generous and he did not contend— all of this sort.
idiomatic: Generous and uncontentious—he was always thus.

literal: He was moved to Chief Clerk to the Shouzhou Grand Governor.
idiomatic: He became chief clerk at Shouzhou.

literal: Yuwen Shu greatly respected him and entrusted him with provincial affairs.
idiomatic: Yuwen Shu respected him and gave him the province's business.

literal: After more than a year he was moved to Inspector of Jin.
idiomatic: A year on he was Inspector of Jin.

literal: In Renshou he was ordered by edict with full powers as Touring Commissioner of the Henan Circuit.
idiomatic: In Renshou he toured Henan circuit with full powers.

literal: On return, because the mission answered the intent, he was made Colonel Third Class and given two hundred rolls of goods.
idiomatic: Returning with a mission that pleased the throne, he was Colonel Third Class with two hundred rolls of goods.

literal: Changheng thought himself at the age of the seventy-year staff and memorialized begging to retire; a gracious edict did not permit it.
idiomatic: Thinking himself at retirement age, he begged to retire; a kind edict refused.

literal: At the start of Daye he was summoned as Left Companion of the Heir Apparent; on the road to Luoyang he died.
idiomatic: Early in Daye he was summoned as the heir's left companion and died on the road to Luoyang.

literal: Sons Baosu and Baoyin.
idiomatic: Sons Baosu and Baoyin.

literal: Daoqian's younger brother Daokan, styled Xizu, was deep, elegant, and devoted to learning; he was Prefectural Clerk and died.
idiomatic: Brother Daokan, styled Xizu, scholarly and refined, was prefectural clerk and died.

literal: Daoyue's son Zhengda was made heir.
idiomatic: Daoyue's son Zhengda was made his heir.

literal: Daokan's younger brother Daohe, styled Shuyong, had the lowest standing among the brothers.
idiomatic: Brother Daohe, styled Shuyong, ranked lowest among the brothers.

literal: He was Army Aide in the Central Army Office of Ji Province and died.
idiomatic: He was army aide in Ji's central staff and died.

literal: His son Jingyou was Administrator of Hongnong.
idiomatic: Son Jingyou was Administrator of Hongnong.

literal: Jingyou's son Shiyan had spirit and bearing; in early Sui Kaihuang he was retainer to Prince Xiu of Shu.
idiomatic: Son Shiyan had force of character; early in Kaihuang he served Prince Xiu of Shu.

literal: Because Xiu's conduct was improper he pleaded illness and ended his days at home.
idiomatic: When Xiu turned lawless he pleaded sickness and died at home.

literal: Daohe's younger brother Daoyue, styled Jigong, was Attendant of the Minister of Works and Grand Rectifier of You.
idiomatic: Brother Daoyue, styled Jigong, was the Minister of Works' attendant and You Grand Rectifier.

literal: At the end of Xinghe he was made Grand General of the Guard and Inspector of Yan; in the province he won men's hearts.
idiomatic: Late in Xinghe he was Grand General of the Guard and Yan inspector and won the province.

literal: He died; posthumously Colonel Third Class and Inspector of You.
idiomatic: He died; posthumously Colonel Third Class and You inspector.

literal: His son Zhengtong had a fine reputation early and was Counselor of the Opening Office; he died.
idiomatic: Son Zhengtong had early fame, was Opening Office counselor, and died.

literal: His wife Lady Xie committed adultery with Zhengtong's younger brother Zhengsi; the censor impeached them and gentlemen despised it.
idiomatic: Wife Lady Xie lay with brother Zhengsi; censors impeached them and gentlemen despised the house.

literal: Zhengsei's younger brother Zhengshan, styled Gongshun, was known early for literature, was Seal Clerk, and attended the Forest of Literature.
idiomatic: Brother Zhengshan, styled Gongshun, was known for letters, seal clerk, Forest of Literature attendant.

literal: The Zhengsi brothers, as maternal uncles of the Qi empress dowager, in Wuping all received generous posthumous gifts.
idiomatic: As the Qi empress dowager's kin, the brothers received lavish posthumous honors in Wuping.

literal: Daoyue's younger brother Daoshu, styled You'an, inherited his father's title and was Gentleman of the Secretariat; he died.
idiomatic: Brother Daoshu, styled You'an, inherited the title, was Secretariat Gentleman, and died.

literal: His son Xiyu inherited.
idiomatic: Son Xiyu inherited.

literal: Xiyu was pure, empty, and kept the Way; he had the air of the ancients and was respected by kin.
idiomatic: Xiyu was pure, held the Way, seemed a man of old times, and kin revered him.

literal: Boyuan's younger brother Min, styled Zhongtong, childhood name Hongya, had great breadth early.
idiomatic: Boyuan's brother Min, styled Zhongtong, childhood name Hongya, was magnanimous from youth.

literal: Xiaowen valued him and took his daughter as a consort.
idiomatic: Xiaowen prized him and took his daughter as consort.

literal: He was Gentleman of Ceremonies, died young, posthumously General of Awesome Far Reach and Administrator of Fanyang; posthumous name Jing.
idiomatic: He was Ceremonies Gentleman, died young, posthumously General of Awesome Far Reach and Fanyang Administrator with posthumous name Jing.

literal: Five sons.
idiomatic: Five sons.

literal: The eldest Yixi, styled Yuanqing, was early devoted to learning; his insight was deep and elegant.
idiomatic: Eldest Yixi, styled Yuanqing, was early scholarly, deep and elegant in judgment.

literal: At nine he lost his father and showed utmost filial nature; young he was admired by Vice Minister Li Chong.
idiomatic: At nine he lost his father and showed perfect filial piety; young he won Li Chong's praise.

literal: He began as Secretariat Gentleman, rose to General Who Overcomes Barbarians and Grand Master of Palace Leisure, and left office for mourning.
idiomatic: He began as Secretariat Gentleman, rose to General Who Overcomes Barbarians and Palace Leisure Grand Master, then mourned his mother.

literal: Inspector Wang Song of You was on close terms with him and often wrote old friends Li Shenjun and others: "General Lu is here; he sometimes favors us and for several days running we may consult on the way of government.
idiomatic: You inspector Wang Song was close and wrote Li Shenjun: "General Lu is here—when he favors us we consult on government for days.

literal: " He was valued to this degree.
idiomatic: Such was his esteem.

literal: Later he was made General Who Punishes Barbarians and Grand Master of the Palace.
idiomatic: Later he was General Who Punishes Barbarians and Palace Grand Master.

literal: For many years he held idle rank and was calm and self-sufficient.
idiomatic: Many years on idle salary he was content.

literal: Li Shenjun urged him to solicit those in power; Yixi said: "Having studied the former kings' Way, one should honor the former kings' will—how can one crudely seek wealth and rank?
idiomatic: Li Shenjun urged him to court the powerful; Yixi said: "I study the former kings' Way—how can I grub for rank and gold?

literal: " In Xiaochang he was made Regular Attendant.
idiomatic: In Xiaochang he was Regular Attendant.

literal: At that time Empress Dowager Ling held court; Palace Attendant Li Shengui's power tilted the court; he sought marriage ties.
idiomatic: Empress Dowager Ling ruled; Li Shengui's power bent the court and he sought a marriage alliance.

literal: Yixi feared he must fail and refused.
idiomatic: Yixi feared ruin and refused.

literal: Wang Song told Yixi: "In olden days men would not trade one daughter for five sons—would you trade?
idiomatic: Wang Song said: "Men once would not trade one daughter for five sons—will you?

literal: " Yixi said: "The reason I do not agree is just this.
idiomatic: Yixi said: "I refuse for exactly that reason.

literal: " Song then grasped Yixi's hand: "I have heard there is fate—do not change it to tell others.
idiomatic: Song seized his hand: "I have heard fate—do not change what I tell you.

literal: " He then married into another clan.
idiomatic: He married elsewhere.

literal: On the eve of the wedding Empress Dowager Ling sent Palace Attendant Fu Jing to his home with an order to stop it; inside and outside were terrified; Yixi was calm as ever.
idiomatic: On the wedding eve Ling sent Fu Jing to halt it; the household panicked; Yixi was unmoved.

literal: In Putai he was made Minister of Justice, General of Agile Cavalry, and Left Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.
idiomatic: In Putai he was Minister of Justice, General of Agile Cavalry, and Left Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.

literal: Yixi was broad, harmonious, cautious, and fearful; he did not make friends lightly.
idiomatic: Yixi was broad, gentle, cautious, and slow to befriend.

literal: His nature was pure and frugal; he did not pursue wealth.
idiomatic: Pure and frugal, he did not chase wealth.

literal: In youth You suffered flood and drought in succession; he had earlier lent tens of thousands of bushels of grain; because the year's grain did not ripen Yixi burned the bonds, and the district rejoiced in his kindness.
idiomatic: You had floods and drought; he had lent tens of thousands of bushels—when grain failed he burned the IOUs and the district blessed him.

literal: Though in a lofty post, whenever he was in want he ate wheat and vegetables and was gladly content.
idiomatic: Though high in office, in want he ate wheat gruel and greens gladly.

literal: He died; posthumously Grand General, Colonel Third Class, and Inspector of Ying; posthumous name Xiaojian.
idiomatic: He died; posthumously Grand General, Colonel Third Class, Ying inspector, posthumous name Xiaojian.

literal: His son Xunzhi was pure, quiet, and free of desire; he was Recorder to the Grand Minister of War.
idiomatic: Son Xunzhi was pure, quiet, without craving, Recorder to the Grand Minister of War.

literal: Yixi's four younger brothers all fell far short of the elder.
idiomatic: Four younger brothers never matched him.

literal: Min's younger brother Chang, styled Shuda, childhood name Shiyan, ranged through classics and histories and had early fame.
idiomatic: Min's brother Chang, styled Shuda, childhood name Shiyan, read widely and was famed early.

literal: In the Taihe era he served concurrently as Supernumerary Regular Attendant on embassy to Qi.
idiomatic: In Taihe he was supernumerary Regular Attendant on embassy to Qi.

literal: Xiaowen instructed Chang: "Close to the Jiang and Yang—sooner or later, not early or late, it will be mine.
idiomatic: Xiaowen told Chang: "Hard by Jiang and Yang—sooner or later it is mine.

literal: You gentlemen may speak if you wish; do not be doubtful or difficult.
idiomatic: Speak freely; do not hold back.

literal: " He also charged Deputy Envoy Wang Qingshi: "Do not let southern speech make you suspect Lu Chang.
idiomatic: He charged deputy Wang Qingshi: "Do not let southern talk make you doubt Lu Chang.

literal: If they already have acquaintances and wish to meet, meet; if discussion is needed, discuss.
idiomatic: If they know someone and wish a meeting, meet; if debate is wanted, debate.

literal: Chang is a mild and gentle gentleman, without much literary talent; if the host orders you to compose verse, do not stop the banquet because Chang does not write.
idiomatic: Chang is a mild gentleman, no great poet—if the host demands verse, do not end the feast because Chang stays silent.

literal: In sending envoys harmony is precious; do not boast against one another in face or bearing.
idiomatic: Envoys should prize harmony, not strut and sneer in each other's faces.

literal: " When they reached Qi, Qi Ming had just taken the throne; Xiaowen campaigned south and Chang's elder brother Boyuan was a general on a separate route.
idiomatic: In Qi, Qi Ming had just risen; Xiaowen marched south while Chang's brother Boyuan led another column.

literal: Because Qi Ming saw the court adding troops, he treated them harshly.
idiomatic: Qi Ming, seeing more Northern Wei troops, treated them harshly.

literal: Chang and the rest were no men of stiff backbone; greatly afraid, tears and sweat ran together.
idiomatic: Chang's party were no iron spines—they shook, wept, and sweated.

literal: Qi Ming supplied them with rotten rice, stinking fish, and chaff beans.
idiomatic: Qi Ming fed them rotten rice, foul fish, and bean husks.
